statement: In people who use drugs in the United States, mostly recruited at harm-reduction services, and in European drug checking studies relayed by one review, people who use test strips or drug checking, compared with people in the same samples who do not, are associated with more fentanyl and heroin use, more injecting, more often having seen an overdose and, in the largest study, already doing more to lower their risk, so simple comparisons of the two groups mix any effect of testing with who chooses to test. At US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips (2023), 414 people who had used strips in the past 30 days and 318 who had not differed in fentanyl use (78 against 59 in 100), injecting (75 against 57 in 100) and ever having been shown how to use strips (76 against 41 in 100); the strip group already reported more of the eight risk-reduction behaviours studied at the start, and its overdose rate was twice as high before allowing for these differences and not clearly different after (risk ratio 2.06, then 1.20). In rural people who inject drugs (2021 to 2023), strip use went with having seen an overdose in the past 6 months (adjusted odds ratio 2.444, 95% CI 1.784 to 3.347), heroin use (1.615, 1.107 to 2.357) and being married or living as married (1.521, 1.084 to 2.134), and less with being unhoused (0.679, 0.504 to 0.913), but not clearly with having overdosed oneself (0.981, 0.676 to 1.424) or with fentanyl use (1.332, 0.948 to 1.872). In a small Rhode Island pilot, the 62 who used a strip differed clearly from the 19 who did not only in more often having sold drugs (84 against 58 in 100), while among those who used a strip, those whose strip showed fentanyl used heroin weekly far more often (20 of 31 against 3 of 31). In three European studies relayed by a review, clients of drug checking services used ecstasy more often than people at the same events who did not use the services. All characteristics were self-reported, and the two larger studies recruited people at harm-reduction services. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: People who use test strips are not the same as people who don't. In US studies they more often used fentanyl or heroin, more often injected and had more often seen an overdose, and in one study they were already doing more to lower their risk before it began. So comparing the two groups cannot tell us what the strips themselves do.
population: People who use drugs in the United States: 732 clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (2023); 541 people who inject drugs at two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia (2021–2023); 81 young adults recruited by advertisement for a Rhode Island pilot (2017); and European drug checking studies relayed by a systematic review
exposure: Using fentanyl test strips (in the past 30 days, or at least one of the strips given) or drug checking services
comparator: People in the same samples who did not use strips or services
outcome: Drug use, injecting, witnessing an overdose, housing, marital status and earlier risk-reduction behaviour, and how an overdose comparison changed after adjustment
magnitude: Vickers-Smith (strip group against no strip): past 30-day fentanyl use 78.2% against 59.2%, injection 75.1% against 56.6%, ever received strip instructions 76.2% against 40.6% (each P < .001), past 30-day overdose 26.0% against 20.5% (P = .10); nonfatal overdose RR 2.06 (1.09–3.89) unadjusted, 1.20 (0.70–2.06) adjusted. Erickson (adjusted odds ratios, full sample): witnessed overdose 2.444 (1.784–3.347), heroin use 1.615 (1.107–2.357), married 1.521 (1.084–2.134), unhoused 0.679 (0.504–0.913), own overdose 0.981 (0.676–1.424), fentanyl use 1.332 (0.948–1.872). Krieger: ever dealt drugs 52/62 (84%) against 11/19 (58%), p = .038; ever injected 29/62 (47%) against 13/19 (68%), p = .099; positive against no positive result: weekly heroin 20/31 (65%) against 3/31 (10%), ever injected 25/31 (81%) against 8/31 (26%), witnessed overdose 29/31 (94%) against 9/31 (29%).

evidence.extracted: At baseline, 414 people who had used strips in the past 30 days and 318 who had not (Table 2): past 30-day fentanyl use 78.2% against 59.2% (698 answering), past 30-day injection 75.1% against 56.6%, ever received strip instructions 76.2% against 40.6% (each P < .001), past 30-day overdose 26.0% against 20.5% (P = .10); people who used strips were more often from Ohio and White and less often from New York, Hispanic or Black.

evidence.extracted: At baseline, people who used strips already had a higher mean composite score and number of overdose risk-reduction behaviours over the past 30 days, and a higher prevalence of nearly every behaviour across most drug categories, except use by routes other than injection, which was more common among people who did not use strips (values in eTables 4 and 5, not read).

evidence.locator: Results › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose; Table 3; Discussion, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Self-reported nonfatal overdose: unadjusted risk ratio 2.06 (95% CI 1.09–3.89) for people who used strips, adjusted 1.20 (0.70–2.06); the authors attribute the change to people who used strips also doing things that raise overdose risk (using several drugs) and things that lower it (testing strength).
evidence.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2833888, searched in the saved page text (scratchpad/vickers_page.txt)

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Model results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Adjusted odds ratios for past-30-day strip use, full sample (541 people) and complete cases (212): witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months 2.444 (95% CI 1.784–3.347) and 2.257 (1.529–3.334); past-30-day heroin use 1.615 (1.107–2.357) and 1.891 (1.178–3.036); married or living as married 1.521 (1.084–2.134) and 1.608 (1.073–2.410); currently unhoused 0.679 (0.504–0.913) and 0.611 (0.410–0.909); own overdose in the past 6 months 0.981 (0.676–1.424) and 0.712 (0.416–1.218); past-30-day fentanyl use 1.332 (0.948–1.872) and 1.357 (0.879–2.095).

The 62 who used a strip and the 19 who did not differed clearly only in ever having dealt drugs (52 of 62, 84%, against 11 of 19, 58%; p = .038); ever injecting was 29 of 62 (47%) against 13 of 19 (68%; p = .099). Among those who used a strip, those with a positive result (31) against those without (31) more often used heroin weekly (20, 65%, against 3, 10%), had ever injected (25, 81%, against 8, 26%) and had ever witnessed an overdose (29, 94%, against 9, 29%) (each p < .001).

evidence.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph
evidence.extracted: In three European cross-sectional studies (Belgium, n = 486, 2006; the Netherlands, n = 285, 2002; Austria, the Netherlands and Germany, n = 702, 2002), clients of drug checking services reported more frequent ecstasy use than people at the same events who did not use the services; in the multi-country study, how often people used the services was negatively correlated with how often they used ecstasy and with unsafe party behaviour.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 140 (first reader), from AI reader 137's study card

evidence.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use, 1st paragraph; Behavior Change from FTS Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: As relayed: drug checking services were more likely to be used by people who had witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months, suspected fentanyl exposure, injected in public, did sex work or had had a nonfatal overdose (one study); people who use drugs often use harm-reduction tools and safer practices whether or not they use strips.

The authors note that the drug checking service may have attracted clients more likely to use harm-reduction strategies, that the data may over-represent clients more likely to have fentanyl in their drugs, and that checks after use may have been prompted by an overdose.

risk_of_bias.note: Strip use and every characteristic were self-reported, usually in the same interviews, so answers that please interviewers could raise both strip use and reported risk reduction; samples of people in contact with services; the Rhode Island comparisons are unadjusted and small.

inconsistency.note: The two larger studies agree (more opioid use and injecting, or more witnessed overdoses, with strip use); the small Rhode Island comparison (19 people without strips) found no clear difference except dealing, and its injecting figures point the other way (47 against 68 in 100, p = .099).

indirectness.note: Rated as a description of who uses strips in these service samples.

imprecision.note: The two larger studies have 732 and 541 people.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; risk of bias takes a level: very low. Rated as worded: differences between people who do and do not use strips in these samples, which matter because they confound comparisons of outcomes (the overdose ratio of 2.06 became 1.20 after adjustment). Status replicated: two independent US cohorts point the same way.
